title: Last valid index
question: An array with zero-based indexing holds 8 elements. Which index refers to the last element?
options: 8, because the last index always equals the total number of elements currently stored in the array
0, because the most recently stored element is always placed back at the start
7, because the first element sits at index 0 and the indexes then run up to length minus one
9, because one extra slot is kept past the end to mark where the array stops
explanation: With zero-based indexing the first element is at index 0, so n elements occupy indexes 0 through n - 1. An index equal to n is already past the end and is an out-of-bounds access. Arrays do not reserve a hidden terminator slot, and new elements are not moved to the front.

title: Memory layout of an array
question: What best describes how a plain fixed-size array stores its elements in memory?
options: In one contiguous block, with every element taking the same amount of space
In scattered blocks, where each element stores the address of the next one
In sorted order, which the memory manager restores whenever it is accessed
In a tree of blocks, where an index selects which branch to follow at each level
explanation: A plain array reserves one contiguous block and each element has the same size, which lets the address of any element be computed directly from its index. Scattered nodes linked by addresses describe a linked list. Arrays are not kept sorted by memory management, and no tree of blocks is involved.

title: Reading past the end
question: In pseudocode, an array a has length 5 and the program reads a[5]. What is the correct way to describe this access?
options: It is valid, because index 5 is simply the fifth position and the array does hold five elements in total
It is valid, because the array grows by one slot whenever a new index is read
It returns the first element, because indexes always wrap around at the array length
It is out of bounds, because the valid indexes are 0 through 4 and index 5 does not exist
explanation: Valid indexes for a length-5 array are 0 to 4, so a[5] lies outside the array. Depending on the language this raises an error or reads unrelated memory, and both outcomes are bugs. Plain arrays never grow on a read, and they do not wrap indexes around unless the code applies a modulo explicitly.

title: When binary search applies
question: Which condition must hold before binary search can correctly find a value in an array?
options: The elements must all be distinct, so that no value ever appears twice
The elements must already be sorted by the same ordering used for comparison
The array length must be a power of two, so each step splits it evenly
The elements must be numbers, because text cannot be compared with less-than
explanation: Binary search discards half of the range by comparing with the middle element, which is only valid when the elements are sorted by the comparison order. Duplicates are fine, and any length works because the middle is rounded. Text can be compared too, as long as an ordering is defined.

title: Substring definition
question: For the string "racecar", which of these is a substring of it?
options: "ceca", because its characters appear next to each other in the original string
"rcar", because its characters appear in the same relative order in the original
"raar", because its characters can all be found somewhere in the original
"cat", because every one of its letters is also a letter of the original
explanation: A substring is a contiguous run of characters, and "ceca" is exactly that (positions 2 to 5). "rcar" keeps the order but skips characters, so it is only a subsequence. "raar" and "cat" merely reuse letters, with "cat" needing a letter that is not even present.

title: The empty string
question: In pseudocode, s is set to "" (two quotes with nothing between them). Which statement about s is correct?
options: It is a missing value, so reading length(s) is an error until it is assigned
It holds a single invisible character, so length(s) is 1 and s[0] is a space
It is a valid string of length 0, which differs from having no string at all
It holds the text "null", so length(s) is 4 and comparisons with it succeed
explanation: The empty string is a real string with zero characters, so length(s) is 0 and it can be concatenated or compared like any other. A missing value (null or none) means there is no string at all, which is a different state. It contains no space or hidden character, and it does not store the word null.

title: Length after concatenation
question: String a has 6 characters and string b has 4. What is true about the result of concatenating a and then b?
options: It has 10 characters, with the characters of a and b alternating one by one
It has 10 characters, with all of a followed immediately by all of b
It has 6 characters, because a concatenation keeps only the longer operand
It has 24 characters, because every character of a is paired with all of b
explanation: Concatenation places the second string right after the first, so lengths add: 6 + 4 = 10, with a's characters first. Interleaving is a different operation, keeping the longer operand discards data, and 24 would be a product, which applies to pairs but not to joining.

title: Hash function consistency
question: Why must a hash table's hash function return the same value every time it receives the same key?
options: Repeated values are needed so that two different keys end up sharing exactly one bucket
Equal outputs let the table skip comparing keys because equal hashes always mean equal keys
A stable value allows the table to keep its entries sorted by key inside every bucket
Randomized results would send a later lookup to a different bucket than the one used to store the key
explanation: A lookup recomputes the hash and goes to that bucket, so a function that changed its answer would look in the wrong place and miss stored keys. Different keys sharing a bucket is a collision to be handled, not a goal. Equal hashes do not prove equal keys, so keys are still compared, and buckets are not required to be sorted.

title: Storing a key twice
question: A hash table maps names to ages. The program stores ("Ana", 30) and later stores ("Ana", 31). What does a standard hash table then return for "Ana"?
options: 31, because a key is unique and the second store replaces the value of the first
30, because the first value is kept and any later store for that same key is silently ignored by the table
Both 30 and 31, because the table keeps every value stored under a key
An error, because a hash table never allows a key to be written more than once
explanation: In a standard map each key appears at most once, so storing under an existing key overwrites its value and a lookup returns 31. Keeping the first value, returning both, or failing are behaviors of other structures or special APIs (a multimap, an insert-if-absent operation, a write-once map), not of the usual put.

title: Why tables resize
question: A hash table keeps adding entries while its bucket count stays fixed. What happens to lookups, and what is the usual remedy?
options: Lookups get faster as buckets fill, so the table is left alone to save memory
Buckets fill up and lookups slow down, so the table grows and redistributes its entries
Lookups stay constant, but keys are lost, so the table must be rebuilt in sorted order
Lookups fail, so the table must switch to a linked list and drop the hash function
explanation: With a fixed bucket count, the average number of entries per bucket (the load factor) keeps rising, so chains or probe sequences lengthen and lookups drift toward linear time. Real tables resize at a threshold and rehash entries into more buckets. Fuller buckets never speed things up, and entries are not lost or required to be sorted.

title: Losing the head reference
question: A singly linked list is accessed only through a variable head. What happens if the program overwrites head with an empty reference without any other copy of it?
options: The list is truncated to its first node, because only head's own node is cleared
The list stays reachable, because every node also stores the position of the head
The nodes become unreachable, because every node is found only by following links from head
The list is sorted automatically, because the structure rebuilds itself from the tail
explanation: Nodes in a linked list are found only by following next links starting from a known node, normally head. Losing the sole reference to head leaves the whole chain unreachable (and in a managed runtime, eligible for garbage collection; elsewhere, leaked). Nodes do not store the head, and nothing rebuilds or sorts the list.

title: What a doubly linked list adds
question: How does a doubly linked list node differ from a singly linked list node?
options: It also stores a link to the previous node, so traversal works in both directions
It stores several values per node, so the list needs fewer nodes for the same data
It stores its index in the list, so any node can be reached without traversal
It stores a link to the head only, so every node can find the start of the list
explanation: Each node of a doubly linked list keeps both next and previous links, which allows backward traversal and removing a node given only that node. It still stores one value per node, it does not track its index (positions shift on insertion), and a link to the head is not what makes the list doubly linked.

title: Reaching the last node
question: A singly linked list has n nodes and keeps only a head reference. What does it take to reach the last node?
options: Constant time, because the head node always stores a direct link to the last node of the list
Logarithmic time, because each step along the links can skip half of the remaining nodes
Constant time, because nodes are stored side by side and can be indexed
Linear time, because the nodes must be followed one link at a time from head
explanation: Without a tail reference the only route to the last node is following next links through all n nodes, which is O(n). A head node links only to its successor, nodes are not contiguous so there is no indexing, and links cannot skip half of the list as a sorted array search would. Keeping a tail reference makes appending O(1).

title: Peek versus pop
question: A stack holds 4, 8, 15 (15 was pushed last). What does the peek operation do?
options: It removes 15 and returns it, shrinking the stack to two elements
It returns 15 and leaves the stack unchanged, still with three elements
It returns 4 and leaves the stack unchanged, still with three elements
It returns the count of elements, which is 3, and leaves the contents alone
explanation: Peek (or top) reads the element on top, here 15, without removing it. Removing and returning it is pop. Reaching 4 would break the last-in, first-out discipline, since that is the oldest element at the bottom, and the number of elements is reported by a separate size operation.

title: The call stack
question: When one function calls another, where does the runtime keep the caller's local variables and return point until the callee finishes?
options: On a call stack, where the callee's frame is pushed on top and popped on return
In a queue of frames, where the oldest pending call is resumed first when the callee ends
In a hash table keyed by function name, so each function can run only once at a time
In a sorted list of frames, ordered by the size of each function's local variables
explanation: Calls nest, so the most recent call must finish first: a stack's last-in, first-out order matches this exactly, and returning pops the callee's frame to resume the caller. A queue would resume the wrong function, and a hash table keyed by name could not hold several active calls of the same function, which recursion needs.

title: Popping an empty stack
question: What is the standard name for the error of popping from a stack that holds no elements?
options: Stack overflow, because removing from an empty stack fills the storage beyond its limit
Hash collision, because two removals are trying to claim the same top position
Stack underflow, because there is no top element left to remove and return
Dangling reference, because the removed element still points at the stack
explanation: Underflow means trying to take from a structure that has nothing left, so popping an empty stack is stack underflow and implementations signal it with an error, an exception or an empty result. Overflow is the opposite condition, pushing onto a full bounded stack. A hash collision belongs to hash tables, and a dangling reference is a different kind of memory bug.

title: Dequeue from an empty queue
question: A queue holds no elements and the program calls dequeue. What is the correct way to describe the situation?
options: It returns the most recently added element, because an empty queue falls back to stack order
It creates an element with a default value, since the queue must always return something
It rotates to the back of the queue, because dequeue always cycles through positions
It is an invalid operation, so the code must check for emptiness or handle the failure
explanation: There is nothing to remove, so dequeue on an empty queue is an underflow and is reported through an error, an exception or an empty result depending on the API; callers should check for emptiness first. A queue never switches to stack order, never invents values, and has no positions to cycle through.

title: Double-ended queue
question: What distinguishes a deque (double-ended queue) from an ordinary queue?
options: It limits insertions to the front and removals to the back, reversing the usual order
It allows adding and removing elements at both the front and the back
It stores its elements in sorted order, so the smallest is always removed first
It holds at most two elements, one at each end, and rejects any further insertion
explanation: A deque supports insertion and removal at both ends, so it can behave as a queue, as a stack or as a mix of both. An ordinary queue inserts at one end and removes at the other, and merely swapping which end is which gives the same structure, not a deque. Sorted removal describes a priority queue, and the name does not limit its capacity to two.

title: Circular array queue
question: A queue is stored in a fixed array with front and back indexes. Why do many implementations make the indexes wrap around to 0 at the end of the array?
options: To reuse the slots freed by dequeues instead of running out of room while the queue is half empty
To keep the elements sorted, because wrapping reorders all of them by their value whenever one is added
To let the queue grow forever, because wrapping adds new slots to the array
To make dequeue remove from the back, because wrapping reverses the direction
explanation: As elements are dequeued the front moves forward, leaving unused slots at the start. Wrapping indexes around lets later enqueues fill them, so a bounded array can serve an unbounded stream as long as the live elements fit. Wrapping does not sort anything, does not enlarge the array, and does not change the first-in, first-out order.

title: Queue in level-by-level traversal
question: A program visits the nodes of a graph level by level, handling every node one step from the start before any node two steps away. Which structure holds the nodes waiting to be visited?
options: A stack, because the most recently discovered node must always be visited first
A sorted array, because nodes must be visited in increasing order of their value
A queue, because the earliest discovered nodes must be visited before later ones
A hash table, because each node is looked up by a key instead of by arrival
explanation: Breadth-first traversal visits nodes in the order they were discovered, which is first-in, first-out, so a queue fits: nodes one step away are enqueued before those two steps away and therefore leave first. A stack gives the depth-first pattern instead. Neither value order nor key lookup relates to distance from the start.
